shipped_row.boundary_rationale: Psalm 131's title names David, “A Song of Ascents. By David.” (web:Ps.131.0 = oshb:Ps.131.1, שִׁ֥יר הַֽמַּֽעֲל֗וֹת לְדָ֫וִ֥ד, byte tier), the part's third such ascription. The body is one humility confession addressed to Yahweh, “Yahweh, my heart isn't arrogant, nor my eyes lofty; nor do I concern myself with great matters, or things too wonderful for me.” (web:Ps.131.1), developed by the weaned-child simile of web:Ps.131.2, and closed by the same imperative summons that ends Psalm 130, “Israel, hope in Yahweh, from this time forward and forever more.” (web:Ps.131.3). At three verses — the fewest of the 15 ascents together with Psalms 133 and 134 — the confession, its simile, and the closing summons to Israel form one uninterrupted movement with no internal address change strong enough to divide it.
shipped_row.strongest_rejected_alternative: A break at web:Ps.131.2/web:Ps.131.3, separating the psalmist's own confession from the closing summons to Israel, was considered but rejected because three verses is too short to support a formal division and the summons functions as the confession's own resolution rather than a new topic.

prev_row.boundary_rationale: web:Ps.130.7 opens the psalm's only address to a second party besides Yahweh across its 8 verses, “Israel, hope in Yahweh, for there is loving kindness with Yahweh. Abundant redemption is with him.” The imperative יַחֵ֥ל יִשְׂרָאֵ֗ל אֶל יְה֫וָה (oshb:Ps.130.7, byte tier, 'Israel, hope in Yahweh') turns the psalm from the personal cry and waiting of web:Ps.130.1-web:Ps.130.6 to a corporate summons, and the closing verse resolves it, “He will redeem Israel from all their sins.” (web:Ps.130.8). Nothing after web:Ps.130.6 returns to the psalmist's own first-person voice, so these two verses form the psalm's second, corporate movement.

next_row.boundary_rationale: Psalm 132's title is the two words “שִׁ֗יר הַֽמַּ֫עֲל֥וֹת” (oshb:Ps.132.1) (a song of ascents; web:Ps.132.0 = oshb:Ps.132.1). The psalm's own opening plea then runs “זְכוֹר יְהוָ֥ה לְדָוִ֑ד” (oshb:Ps.132.1) -- “Yahweh, remember David and all his affliction,” (web:Ps.132.1) -- where the third word sits as the indirect object of the verb “remember,” not a le-David attribution formula naming an author; the genre label itself carries no name. This opening plea leads into a report of David's own self-imprecating oath, introduced by “נִ֭שְׁבַּע” (oshb:Ps.132.2) (“he swore”) and voiced in direct quotation from “אִם אָ֭בֹא בְּאֹ֣הֶל בֵּיתִ֑י” (oshb:Ps.132.3) (“Surely I will not come into the structure of my house,” web:Ps.132.3) through the close of web:Ps.132.5, where the quotation mark shuts (“until I find out a place for Yahweh, a dwelling for the Mighty One of Jacob.”). The row spans the invocation and this initial quoted oath as one movement; the quotation's own close before the unquoted “Behold, we heard of it in Ephrathah.” (web:Ps.132.6) marks the row's far seam.
next_row.strongest_rejected_alternative: Opening web:Ps.132.1 alone as its own row was considered, since it is the psalm's own plea distinct from the oath report that follows; rejected because the plea has no independent tier-1 close of its own -- the oath-report verb of 132:2 continues its clause without a fresh vocative or quotation boundary.

shipped_row.boundary_rationale: Untitled, Psalm 135 opens “הַ֥לְלוּ יָ֨הּ הַֽ֭לְלוּ אֶת שֵׁ֣ם יְהוָ֑ה” (oshb:Ps.135.1) -- “Praise Yah! Praise Yahweh's name! Praise him, you servants of Yahweh,” (web:Ps.135.1) -- an imperative call to praise that continues through web:Ps.135.3's own hallelu-Yah (“Praise Yah, for Yahweh is good. Sing praises to his name, for that is pleasant.”), then supplies an opening motive for praise, “For Yah has chosen Jacob for himself, Israel for his own possession.” (web:Ps.135.4). The psalm's hallelu-Yah frame opens here in both its occurrences (verse-initial at 135:1 and 135:3, per psalm_device_inventory.json's halleluyah inventory) and, on that inventory, recurs verse-finally at the psalm's own close -- a frame this opening row does not itself carry evidence for past its own span.
shipped_row.strongest_rejected_alternative: Ending the row at 135:3, keeping just the imperative praise-calls together, was considered and is a serious rival reading. The particle "for" that opens both 135:4 and 135:5 stands on both sides of the 4|5 seam and is absent from 135:3's own opening, so it cannot itself be the reason a seam falls at 3|4 rather than 4|5 -- as a shared particle it argues for extending the rival span through 135:4, not against it. The stronger reason to keep 135:4 with this row instead is 135:5's own first-person-singular opening (oshb:Ps.135.5: כִּ֤י אֲנִ֣י, 'for I'), which launches an eight-verse third-person-dominant unit that 135:4's own motive clause does not share.

prev_row.boundary_rationale: Psalm 134's title repeats 132's own wording, bare shir hamma'alot with no name attached (web:Ps.134.0 = oshb:Ps.134.1). Its three verses form one antiphonal exchange: an imperative call to the night-watch temple servants, “Look! Praise Yahweh, all you servants of Yahweh, who stand by night in Yahweh's house!” (web:Ps.134.1), continuing “Lift up your hands in the sanctuary. Praise Yahweh!” (web:Ps.134.2), (בָּרֲכ֣וּ אֶת יְ֭הוָה, oshb:Ps.134.1, the imperative 'bless Yahweh', which WEB renders 'praise'; וּ֝בָרֲכוּ אֶת יְהוָֽה, oshb:Ps.134.2, the same 2mp imperative repeated), then a reply that reverses the direction of blessing: “יְבָרֶכְךָ֣ יְ֭הוָה מִצִּיּ֑וֹן” (oshb:Ps.134.3) -- “May Yahweh bless you from Zion, even he who made heaven and earth.” (web:Ps.134.3). The same root now stands 3ms with a 2ms object suffix ('he will bless you'). The call (134:1-2) addresses the servants in the imperative; the reply (134:3) turns the blessing back onto whoever has just spoken it, closing the short ascents collection's coda with this exchange rather than a further imperative.
prev_row.strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating 134:1-2 and 134:3 as two rows was considered, since the addressee reverses between them (servants addressed, then the worshipper blessed); rejected because three verses is too little to divide without padding, and no vocative, quotation, or report boundary marks an independent seam between the call and its answer.

The row closes where the psalm's address turns from Egypt (135:9) to Yahweh by name at web:Ps.135.13 (“Your name, Yahweh, endures forever”) -- an addressee-identity shift, not a person-number one, since 135:9 already carries second-person address inside this row's own span.

next_row.boundary_rationale: “עֲצַבֵּ֣י הַ֭גּוֹיִם כֶּ֣סֶף וְזָהָ֑ב” (oshb:Ps.135.15) -- “The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of men's hands.” (web:Ps.135.15) -- opens an idol polemic that runs through mouths that cannot speak and eyes that cannot see (web:Ps.135.16), ears that cannot hear (web:Ps.135.17), to the closing verdict, “Those who make them will be like them, yes, everyone who trusts in them.” (web:Ps.135.18). This four-verse unit shows cross-psalm texture with Ps 115's idol polemic (115:4-115:8): a word-by-word byte comparison of both psalms' own text (verse_map_oshb.json) finds oshb:Ps.135.16 matching oshb:Ps.115.5 and oshb:Ps.135.18 matching oshb:Ps.115.8 letter-for-letter, while 135:15's construct chain with the article (עֲצַבֵּ֣י הַ֭גּוֹיִם) differs from 115:4's suffixed plural (oshb:Ps.115.4: עֲֽ֭צַבֵּיהֶם), and 135:17's own clause (oshb:Ps.135.17: אָזְנַ֣יִם לָ֭הֶם וְלֹ֣א יַאֲזִ֑ינוּ) is longer than 115:6 alone on all 3 measures taken (skeleton words, consonants, codepoints), running shorter only against 115:6-115:7 combined, and substitutes a different verb root (יַאֲזִ֑ינוּ for oshb:Ps.115.6's יִשְׁמָ֑עוּ) inside the clause the two verses share. It is discussed here as a recognizable, recurring cross-psalm texture, not merged with Ps 115's own rows.
